if (!/before|register.{0,30}first|timer first/i.test(output)) throw new Error('says register the timer before the business operation');
return true;

response.output:
Register the timer first, then run the business operation.

- **Why:** if timer registration fails, nothing has happened yet, so no work goes untracked. If you did it the other way round, the operation could succeed and then the timer registration could fail, which leaves an order with no expiration.
- **The cost:** the timer can fire when the operation never completed. Make the target handle that by returning `effects().done()` for not-found, already-cancelled and invalid cases. A target that errors on those cases reschedules forever.
- **Name and idempotency:** use a deterministic name like `"order-expiration-" + orderId`. Re-scheduling the same name replaces the existing timer, so retries don't pile up duplicates. Also make the target idempotent, because delivery is at-least-once.

if (!/stable|component id|method name|serial|break|cannot (be )?resolv|orphan|fail/i.test(output)) throw new Error('warns the serialized timer stores component id and method name');
return true;

response.output:
Yes. Any timer scheduled before the deploy still points at the old component id and method name, because the runtime stores **component id + method name + parameter**. After the deploy those calls no longer resolve, so they fail and reschedule with backoff (about 3s, capped around 30s) indefinitely. The timers never fire the intended work, such as order expiration. They also keep retrying and count against the 50,000-timer limit.

**Fix:**
- Keep the old component id and old method in place as a shim. Have it delegate to the new method, or make it `return effects().done();` if the work is obsolete.
- Leave the shim in until `akka services components list-timers <service> -o json` shows no timers referencing the old id or method.
- New timers can use the new id and method straight away.

If the deploy is already out, redeploy with the shim. Pending timers will then resolve on their next retry. Alternatively, re-schedule them under the same deterministic timer name, which replaces the old entry. That only works if you can enumerate the affected ids.

Also check the payload. If the parameter type changed too, the same problem applies.
